The word mogul has three distinct meanings in modern English. You need to know all three to truly understand this word.
Meaning 1: A Very Powerful and Influential Person

This is by far the most common way the word is used today. A mogul is someone who has reached an extraordinary level of power, wealth, and influence — usually within a specific industry. The word implies that this person doesn't just work in their field; they dominate it. They make big decisions, control large amounts of money, and have the kind of authority that shapes the industry around them.

Think of it this way: in any major industry — film, music, tech, media, real estate — there are thousands of ordinary workers, hundreds of managers, dozens of executives, and then at the very top, a tiny handful of people who seem to own the whole game. Those people at the absolute top are moguls.

Examples in sentences:

  • "He built his company from nothing and became a media mogul, owning dozens of TV channels and newspapers."
  • "The Hollywood moguls decide which movies get made and which ones never see the light of day."
  • "She is a real estate mogul who owns property in nearly every major city in the world."

Important nuance: The word carries a strong flavor of dominance and control, not just wealth. A billionaire who quietly invests money might not be called a mogul. But someone who actively runs and controls a major part of an industry usually is. The word often has a slightly dramatic, larger-than-life feeling to it — moguls are people who loom large.

When written with a capital M, Mogul refers historically to the emperors of the Mughal Empire, which ruled much of the Indian subcontinent from the early 1500s to the 1800s. These emperors — such as Akbar, Shah Jahan (who built the Taj Mahal), and Aurangzeb — were among the wealthiest and most powerful rulers in the entire world during their time.

The term The Great Mogul or The Grand Mogul was specifically used by Europeans to refer to these emperors. Their reputation for breathtaking wealth and absolute power was so legendary across the world that over time, the word mogul in general English began to mean simply a supremely powerful person — which is how Meaning 1 was born.

Today, this historical usage is mostly found in history books and academic discussions. In everyday conversation, when someone says "mogul," they almost always mean Meaning 1.
Meaning 3: A Bump on a Ski Slope

In the world of skiing, a mogul is something completely different — it is a rounded, hard mound of snow that forms on a ski slope. Moguls are not artificial obstacles placed there by resort staff. They form naturally over time as many skiers repeatedly turn in the same spots, pushing the snow into bumps. The result is a slope covered in a field of these uneven lumpy mounds, which makes skiing down it significantly more challenging and physically demanding.

Skiing through a field of moguls requires a specific technique: the knees act as shock absorbers, bending and extending rapidly as the skier rolls over each bump. It is a skill that takes considerable practice.

Mogul skiing is actually a recognized competitive sport and has been an official Olympic event since 1992, falling under the category of freestyle skiing. Competitors are judged on their speed, the quality of two aerial jumps they perform mid-run, and the technical precision of their turns through the bumps.

Examples in sentences:

  • "The steep slope was covered in moguls, making it one of the most difficult runs at the resort."
  • "She trained for years to compete in mogul skiing at the Winter Olympics."

What it means
Mogul (in business/society)A supremely powerful, wealthy, and dominant person in an industry
Mogul (historical, capital M)An emperor of the Mughal Empire of India
Mogul (in skiing)A rounded bump of hard snow on a ski slope

The business meaning is the one you will encounter constantly in news, books, and conversation. The skiing meaning is common in sports contexts. The historical meaning is mostly limited to history. All three are correct, standard uses of the same word — context will always make it clear which one is meant.
